description:
Hub <-> agent wire protocol, version 1. The one definition of the messages.

The channel is a websocket at ``/api/v1/agent``; the agent authenticates the
upgrade request with ``Authorization: Bearer <rig join token>``. Every message
is one JSON object, one websocket frame::

    {"v": 1, "type": "<type>", "id": "<sender-chosen id>", "re": "<id>", "body": {}}

``re`` names the message being answered; ``body`` is type-specific.

Liveness. Agent -> hub: ``hello`` (first message: identity, live hardware, and
optionally the models on disk, capabilities and candidate network endpoints;
re-send it whenever the inventory changes) and ``heartbeat`` (periodic, optional
fresh readings). The hub acks each; the hello ack carries the heartbeat
interval. A fatal ``error`` is followed by a close with a ``CloseCode``.

Sessions (pooled inference). The hub sends session commands only to agents whose
hello carried ``capabilities``. A rig runs one session at a time, or, with
``multi_session``, up to ``MAX_SESSIONS_REPORTED`` at once on different cards;
ids are hub-chosen. Each command is answered, with ``re`` = the command's
``id``, by ``ack`` (done or accepted) or ``error`` (refused; ``code`` says
why), except ``session_prepare`` (answered by ``session_prepared``) and
``session_query`` (by ``session_status``).
Every command is idempotent: repeating it with the same arguments gives the
same answer and changes nothing more, so the hub may retry after a timeout.

- ``session_prepare`` -> ``session_prepared``: make (or return the existing)
  ephemeral WireGuard keypair for the session; reply with the public key, the
  listen port and candidate endpoints. Private keys never leave the rig.
- ``tunnel_up`` -> ``ack``: configure the tunnel: own address, peers' public
  keys, endpoint candidates and allowed IPs. Rig-to-rig traffic stays in it.
- ``worker_start`` -> ``ack``: start an RPC server per listed card, bound to the
  tunnel address only; ``session_status`` ``ready`` follows when listening.
- ``head_start`` -> ``ack``: start the model server with exactly this ordered
  device list and tensor split (``tensor_split[i]`` is device ``i``'s share);
  ``session_status`` ``loading`` then ``ready`` or ``failed`` follow. The model
  is named, never a path: the agent resolves it in its own inventory. The last
  device holds the output layer, so the hub puts a card of the head rig itself
  last unless the model fits only with a worker's card there. ``slots`` is how
  many requests the server serves at once and ``ctx`` the context of each, so
  the server runs ``slots`` slots of ``ctx`` tokens each (llama.cpp: ``-np
  slots -c slots*ctx``, never a unified KV cache).
- ``session_query`` -> ``session_status``; ``session_stop`` -> ``ack`` (also for
  unknown or already stopped sessions). The agent may send ``session_status``
  unprompted at any time (progress, crash). ``log_excerpt`` is bounded and
  shown to session participants; the hub replaces control characters.

Relay (one OpenAI-compatible API request to the head's local server). Hub:
``relay_request`` then ``relay_data`` frames (seq 0, 1, ...) carrying exactly
``body_bytes`` request bytes. Agent: ``relay_response`` (status, content type),
``relay_data`` frames with the response bytes, then exactly one ``relay_end``.
The agent answers every ``relay_request`` with a ``relay_end`` (a refusal is a
``relay_end`` with outcome ``error`` and an ``error_code``). Flow control: the
agent may have at most ``window`` response ``relay_data`` frames not yet
credited; the hub returns credit with ``relay_credit`` as it forwards them, and
the agent stops reading upstream while out of credit. ``relay_cancel`` aborts
(the agent still ends with ``relay_end``). Both sides enforce ``timeout_s``
and ``max_response_bytes``. A ``request_id`` is never reused; a relay is retried
only with a new id. ``relay_data`` carries raw bytes as base64, so UTF-8
sequences may be split across frames.

Features. ``capabilities.features`` (an open set) names optional behaviours;
the hub uses one only with an agent that lists it, so an agent without them
keeps working as before:

- ``probe``: answers ``probe_open`` and ``probe_run`` (the latency probe);
- ``traversal``: gathers its WireGuard port's reflexive address when
  ``session_prepare`` carries ``traversal``, walks ``tunnel_up`` candidates in
  order with the relay as the last resort, and answers ``tunnel_up`` with
  ``tunnel_report`` instead of ``ack``;
- ``head_slots``: starts a head with ``head_start.slots`` request slots and
  serves that many relays at once. The hub sends ``slots`` > 1 only to an
  agent that lists it; an agent without it would drop the field and serve one;
- ``hitchhike_units``: advertises the units its host runs for themselves and
  shares with riders (``unit_advert``), and serves rides to them
  (``unit_relay_request``); see Hitchhiking below.
- ``multi_session``: runs several sessions at once, at most
  ``MAX_SESSIONS_REPORTED``, never two on one card: each holds the cards its
  ``worker_start`` or ``head_start`` named, and its own tunnel port (in its
  ``session_prepared``), until its teardown is done. A start naming a card
  another session holds is refused ``busy`` and starts nothing, as is a
  ``session_prepare`` when every lent card or every tunnel port is held. An
  agent without it runs one session at a time and refuses another ``busy``.

An agent without ``traversal`` answers ``tunnel_up`` with ``ack`` and uses LAN
candidates only; the hub pairs it only with rigs behind the same public
address as itself. ``hello.weight_cache`` lists the digests of model weights a
worker keeps from earlier sessions; ``worker_start.model`` names the weights a
session loads (the head's file), and a worker may serve from its cache only
weights with that digest (else ``model_mismatch``).

Reconnect. When an agent's link drops, the hub keeps that rig's sessions for
``RECONNECT_GRACE_S`` seconds: a hello within it that lists a session in
``sessions`` resumes it; a hello that does not, or no hello in time, fails
it. Relays in flight on a dropped link fail at once. After a session stops,
the agent sends a ``heartbeat`` as soon as the memory is freed; until then the
hub treats the rig's readings as stale.

Hitchhiking (``hitchhike_units``). A host runs their own units (their own
ladder's model servers) and shares open slots of them with riders the hub
matches. The agent sends ``unit_advert`` with every unit it shares, the whole
set each time (an empty list withdraws them all): after its hello is acked,
whenever the set or a unit's ``free_slots`` changes (at most once a second),
and at least every ``UNIT_ADVERT_INTERVAL_S`` seconds. The hub acks it,
treats an advert older than ``UNIT_ADVERT_STALE_S`` as withdrawn and forgets
it when the link drops. Per unit: a ``unit_id`` the agent chooses (stable
while the unit's setup is unchanged), its ``model`` (as requests name it and
answers carry it; one unit per model), its ``slots`` and the ``ctx`` of each,
``free_slots`` (the slots the host's own requests leave free now; rides are
not subtracted) and ``rider_cap`` (the most rides at once the host allows,
below ``slots``: the host keeps one). ``unit_relay_request`` is a
``relay_request`` aimed at an advertised unit (``unit_id`` in place of
``session_id``), followed by the same frames, by ``request_id`` (one id space
with ``relay_request``). Its body names the unit's ``model``; the agent
passes it unchanged to the unit's own address, and the answer back as the
unit gives it. The host's own requests go first, and a free slot is enough:
a ride is admitted while the unit has a free slot (the host's own requests
in flight and the rides on it together take fewer than ``slots``) and the
rides on it are fewer than ``rider_cap``; no slot is kept free for the host
beyond that. The hub sends a ride by that rule on the last advert's count
(``slots - free_slots`` for the host's own requests). The agent, which reads
the unit's count as the ride arrives, decides last: it refuses a ride
(``relay_end``, outcome ``error``) with ``unknown_unit`` (no unit of that id
advertised), or ``busy`` when ``rider_cap`` rides run on the unit or it has
no free slot.

Latency probe (``probe``). Before planning, the hub measures rig-to-rig paths
it has no fresh figures for, a bounded number at a time. ``probe_open``
(``token``, the hub's ``stun`` endpoints, ``ttl_s``) -> ``probe_opened``: the rig
opens one UDP socket for the probe, sends a binding request (below) from it
to each ``stun`` endpoint, and answers with that socket's candidate endpoints
(``lan``, ``ipv6``) and its round trip to the responder. ``probe_run`` ->
``probe_result``, sent to every rig of the probe at once: each rig sends
``count`` pings ``interval_ms`` apart to every candidate of every peer at once
(which also opens its NAT to the peer's pings) and answers the peers' pings;
then, if ``bulk_bytes`` > 0, it sends that many bytes as bulk packets to the
peer's first answering candidate. Within ``deadline_ms`` it reports per peer
whether a candidate answered, which, the median and least round trip, the
loss, and the rate at which the peer's bulk packets arrived. The socket
closes after ``ttl_s``.

NAT traversal (``traversal``). A multi-rig session's tunnel is opened so:

1. ``session_prepare.traversal`` (``token``, ``stun``): the rig sends binding
   requests from its WireGuard listen port to each ``stun`` endpoint. The
   hub's responder answers with the source address it saw and records it
   against the token: the hub learns each rig's reflexive candidate first
   hand, and from two responder ports whether the NAT maps per destination
   ("symmetric", which hole punching cannot cross).
2. The hub orders each peer's candidates: LAN addresses only when both rigs
   share a public address; then IPv6; then the reflexive address (dropped
   when both NATs are symmetric). It forwards only candidates it can vouch
   for (a private LAN address, or an address it observed itself), so no rig
   can aim its peers' packets at a third party. A peer may carry a ``relay``
   grant.
3. ``tunnel_up`` goes to all members in the same moment. Each rig walks each
   peer's candidates in order, ``attempt_s`` per candidate, sending WireGuard
   handshakes; both sides do, so each side's first packets open its NAT for
   the other's (simultaneous hole punching). A completed WireGuard handshake
   confirms a path. If none completes, the rig binds to the peer's relay
   grant (below) and points that peer at the relay. Within
   ``connect_timeout_s`` it answers ``tunnel_report`` with each peer's ``path``
   (``lan``, ``ipv6``, ``direct``, ``relay`` or ``none``; an open set), the
   endpoint used and the handshake round trip; it may send ``tunnel_report``
   unprompted later when a path changes.

Relay. A small UDP forwarder, next to the hub or elsewhere, carries opaque
WireGuard packets between the two rigs of a pair; it holds no keys, so the
traffic stays end-to-end encrypted. A grant's ``ticket`` is opaque to rigs: it
names the pair and side, expires and caps bytes, and the relay checks it with
a key it shares with the hub. The rig sends a relay bind with the ticket to
the grant's host and port; the relay answers with the UDP port of the rig's
side, admits the bind's source IP address there, and latches the first packet
from that address as the rig's endpoint (a new bind re-latches). The rig sets
the peer's WireGuard endpoint to the grant host and that port. The relay
forwards packet for packet between the two latched endpoints, nothing else.

UDP formats (big-endian). Tokens and secrets are 16 random bytes, written in
messages as 32 hex digits. A request is padded so that no answer is larger
than it; a packet without a valid token, secret or ticket gets no answer::

    binding request  "MCGS" 01 01 0000 token[16] txid[12] zeros (64-512 bytes)
    binding answer   "MCGS" 01 02 family(04|06) 00 txid[12] port[2] address
    probe packet     "MCGP" 01 kind 0000 secret[16] seq[4] stamp[8] padding
                     (36-1200 bytes; kind 01 ping, 02 pong: the ping echoed,
                     same length, seq and stamp; 03 bulk: stamp = packets in
                     the train)
    relay bind       "MCGR" 01 01 length[2] ticket zeros (96-512 bytes)
    relay answer     "MCGR" 01 02 port[2] (bound) | "MCGR" 01 03 reason[1]

Endpoint kinds (an open set): ``lan``, ``public`` (named by the owner),
``reflexive``, ``ipv6``, ``relay``, ``stun`` (the hub's responder).

Compatibility and versioning:

- additive changes (new message types, new optional fields) keep ``v`` = 1;
- receivers ignore unknown fields;
- a receiver answers an unknown ``type`` with ``error`` code ``unsupported_type``
  and keeps the connection open;
- error ``code`` is an open set of snake_case strings (``ErrorCode`` lists the
  current ones); agents must tolerate codes they do not know;
- closed sets (session states, roles, device kinds, relay outcomes) only grow
  by adding a new optional field or message type, never by new values that old
  receivers would reject;
- breaking changes bump ``v``; a hub rejects versions it does not speak with
  ``unsupported_version``.

So a receiver validates every frame against ``Envelope`` (open to future types),
then dispatches on ``type`` and validates the types it knows. Send at most
``MAX_FRAMES_PER_SECOND`` frames per second; the hub closes floods.

The agent is a separate stdlib-only codebase; it consumes the JSON Schema
written by ``render_json_schema`` (checked in at schemas/protocol.schema.json).
